newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Moody's team starts review of Pakistan economy.
newsitem.headline: Moody's team starts review of Pakistan economy.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service credit agency, that has threatened to cut Pakistani ratings, began talks with officials in Islamabad on Monday, a business source said.
Moody's said last month it might cut Pakistan's B1 long-term foreign currency rating and its B2 sovereign ceiling for foreign currency deposits.
Pakistan's B1-rated foreign currency bonds and notes were also placed on review for possible downgrade.

The source said Moody's senior rating analysts David Levy and Kristin Lindow had met finance ministry officials and were expected to meet Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's top economic advisers V.A. Jafarey and Shahid Hasan Khan on Tuesday.
They also planned to meet former finance minister Sartaj Aziz, secretary general and main economic spokesman for the opposition Pakistan Muslim League party on Tuesday.

Moody's had voiced concern at "Pakistan's weakening macroeconomic fundamentals, as evidenced by the deviations from long-standing goals of economic restructuring, as well as increased levels of short-term debt and ongoing balance of payments difficulties".
The government hopes that its agreement on an economic rescue package with the International Monetary Fund will dissuade Moody's from downgrading the ratings.
Details of the measures, aimed at persuading the IMF to reactivate a stalled $600 million standby loan, are expected to be announced before an IMF mission arrives on Thursday.
The new measures, expected to include imposition of an agricultural income tax, are likely to meet stiff resistance from politically powerful landlords.

Pakistan, faced with a yawning current account deficit and shrinking foreign reserves, is under IMF pressure to reduce its budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product from anywhere between five and six percent in 1995/96 (July-June).
